title: Salt in the water
word: the whole five years in seven sits
hookLine: a father, a cup of salt water, and the line under year two: you are that
carry: tat tvam asi: the self in you is Brahman
tomorrow: year three: whose great story walks in next?

cards: A favorite song sounds different the first time it's heard on good headphones: a bass line, a second voice, a whole layer that was always there underneath. Year two of this path was that layer.
After a year of first words and stories, it opened the texts underneath them: the big Upanishads, Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana read part by part.
And the most well-known lesson in all of it took nothing but a cup of salty water.

teach.h: SALT IN WATER, GONE FROM SIGHT.
teach.b: In the Chandogya, the sage Uddalaka has a son, Shvetaketu, who comes home after twelve years of study rather proud of himself. So his father gives him a lesson with no book.
Put this salt in water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. In the morning: where's the salt? The boy looks.
It's gone. Sip from this edge, says the father. How is it?
From the far edge? Salty. You can't see it, the father says, but it's there in every drop.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: YOU ARE THAT.
teach.b: That finest essence is in all that is. That is the real. That is the self.
And you are that, Shvetaketu. Tat tvam asi.

teach.h: BRAHMAN IN EVERYTHING, AND IN YOU.
teach.b: This is the heart of the Upanishads: Brahman, the one reality, is in everything, and the self in you, the atman, is not apart from it.

Year two found the same depth elsewhere: Patanjali defining yoga as the stilling of the mind's turnings, Valmiki's Ramayana read for itself. And this year, tat tvam asi came back as one of the four great sayings.
Now this week, in one breath. Hear what is good. The power in your senses is Brahman's.
Words match mind. The self is not the body. Teacher as god.
Ganesha first. And: you are that.

how: Students who move from the stories to the texts often read the Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras and Valmiki's Ramayana in translation, a passage at a time, sometimes with a teacher or a study group.

games.q: what does “the whole five years in seven sits” mean?
o: a retreat of silent days spent in a row
a look back at the whole path, from the top
a final exam taken before graduation

games.q: year two, under the stories. tap the pairs.
p: the Ramayana, read part by part

s: Shvetaketu could still see the salt in the morning
it had dissolved; he couldn't see it, but every sip tasted of it.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras begin with physical poses
they open by defining yoga as the stilling of the mind's turnings.
tat tvam asi, from year two's Chandogya, came back this year as one of the four great sayings
the roots of the summit were planted in year two.

games.q: your little cousin asks, 'if God is real, where is he? I can't see him.' which story from year two answers that?
o: Uddalaka's salt in water: unseen, yet in every sip. tat tvam asi.
Patanjali's poses: God is found by stretching the right way.
none; Hindus say God is only in the temple.
games.why: the salt can't be seen but is tasted everywhere. the Chandogya says that finest essence is in all things, and in you.

practice: If there's a glass of water near you, take one slow sip and remember Uddalaka's cup: the salt unseen, and in every drop. Then, if there's paper near you, write one line from this path that has stayed with you, in your own hand.
Read it back slowly, once, and rest with it.

wordCard.voice: The second look back, to year two: the texts under the stories, and a father who taught his son with salt.

orig.note: Sanskrit: you are that; the Chandogya's refrain, met in year two and again this year.

carryVoice: To carry: tat tvam asi, the self in you is Brahman. The salt is in every sip. That's the week.
